restatements.text: Names the measure the Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026.

Declares that Californians face high costs and taxes, that government programs suffer from inefficiency and waste, and that new taxes should not be exempt from the voter-approved state spending limit.

States the measure's purpose is to require the California State Auditor to perform audits on programs receiving new special taxes, share results with the public, and prohibit exemptions from the state spending limit.

Adds Article XXIV to the California Constitution. Requires the California State Auditor to conduct a pre-election financial and performance audit of programs proposed to receive special tax revenues via initiative. Specifies 10 criteria the audit must cover, requires an executive summary in the state voter information guide, and mandates that audit costs be reimbursed from the special tax revenue if the measure passes.

Requires the California State Auditor to conduct ongoing financial and performance audits every four years for all programs receiving special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, reimbursed from the tax revenue.
Prohibits the state from imposing, collecting, or enforcing any state tax enacted on or after January 1, 2026, if that tax is exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation.

Defines key terms, including 'Government Spending Limitation' as Article XIII B, and 'exempted or excluded' as depositing revenues outside the General Fund where appropriations are not subject to the limit or increasing the limit by statute.
Applies the article to all statewide initiatives submitted on or after January 1, 2026.

Declares that if this measure receives more votes, it nullifies any other measure on the same ballot that imposes different audit rules on special taxes or contains a tax exempt from the Government Spending Limitation.
Makes the act effective and operative at the earliest possible date allowed by the Constitution.
Requires liberal construction to effectuate its intent.

Requires the Attorney General to appoint an independent counsel to defend the act if both the Governor and Attorney General refuse to do so, and creates a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to cover these legal costs.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. Based on the measure text alone, it adds mandatory pre-election audits and voter guide summaries for special tax initiatives.
Current law was not provided. Based on the measure text alone, it introduces mandatory ongoing performance and financial audits every four years for programs receiving new special taxes.
Current law was not provided. Based on the measure text alone, it expressly prevents any new state tax from being exempted from the existing Government Spending Limitation (Article XIII B).

There are direct costs to the state for the Auditor to perform comprehensive pre-election audits. These costs are reimbursed from the special tax revenue if passed, meaning the intended program receives less net funding.

There is a significant opportunity cost: by disallowing exemptions from the spending cap, the state cannot use new tax revenues for programs once the overall spending limit is reached, potentially starving services of new funding.

Programs funded by the special tax bear the cost by having audit expenses deducted from their revenue. The State Auditor benefits from a guaranteed reimbursement stream. Taxpayers benefit from increased transparency.

By eliminating the ability to exempt new taxes from the spending limit, lawmakers or initiative proponents may be disincentivized from pursuing special taxes and might seek alternate revenue forms like fees, or face automatic rebates if the state reaches its spending limit.

The text asserts problems of government inefficiency, waste, and special interests bypassing spending limits to raise taxes. It addresses these through mandatory detailed audits, voter disclosures, and a hard prohibition on exempting new taxes from the spending limit.
The California State Auditor gains substantial investigative power and a dedicated funding stream. Elected officials lose the power to maneuver new taxes around the state spending limit.

It is disputed whether strict constitutional spending limits force government to become more efficient or whether they merely restrict necessary public investment during periods of need, with economists and researchers divided on the net impact.
An appointed independent counsel gains the power to defend the law, reducing the discretion historically held by the Governor and Attorney General.
Because it adds Article XXIV to the California Constitution, it can only be undone or amended by another constitutional amendment approved by voters.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law, the Attorney General shall appoint independent counsel
flags.note: Overrides existing law regarding the Attorney General's exclusive authority or discretion to defend state law.

flags.quote: The provisions of this Act are severable. If any portion, section, subdivision, paragraph, clause, subclause, sentence, phrase, word, or application of this Act is for any reason held to be invalid by a decision of any court of competent jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect the validity of the remaining portions of this Act.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution. This Act shall become operative on the same day it takes effect.
flags.note: Specifies the effective date of the act.
